title: "Helmert coding"

Some categorical predictors have an order that licenses planned comparisons. [**Helmert coding**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=133) compares each later level with the average of earlier levels.

The fitted row contributions factor under the same [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) assumption as the underlying regression. Coding changes comparisons among recorded MALD item groups; it does not change their selection process or create experimental independence.

Recall from [contrast coding](coding-categorical-predictors.qmd) that a coding column assigns one numerical weight to each category, and the coefficient meaning follows from those weights. Helmert coding is useful when the categories have a meaningful order and our question concerns successive stages in that order.

## Ordered syllable bands in MALD

We group item syllable counts into one, two, three, and four-or-more syllables. The open top band is internally heterogeneous, so these contrasts do not represent equal one-syllable steps.

A linguistic hypothesis might predict a first complexity cost from one to two syllables, then ask whether three-syllable words differ from the average of shorter words and whether the open-ended long-word band differs from all earlier bands. That ordered hypothesis licenses Helmert contrasts. If the question instead concerns a constant change per syllable, a numeric predictor is the more direct restriction.

R's Helmert matrix for the observed band order is

$$
\begin{array}{c|rrr}
&H_1&H_2&H_3\\\hline % dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
1&-1&-1&-1\\
2&1&-1&-1\\
3&0&2&-1\\ % dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
4+&0&0&3 % dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
\end{array}.
$$

The columns compare two versus one, three versus the earlier-band average, and four-or-more versus the earlier-band average. Because the columns are not divided by their squared lengths, coefficient magnitude depends on this displayed scaling.

Work through the second column. Its weights are $-1$, $-1$, $2$, and $0$. The zero leaves the final band out of the comparison. The two negative weights combine the first two bands, while the positive weight singles out the third. Because the weights sum to zero, a common upward shift in every fitted band mean cancels and the column retains only a comparison among bands.

Let the four adjusted band means be $m_1,m_2,m_3,$ and $m_{4+}$. The named differences are $m_2-m_1$, $m_3-(m_1+m_2)/2$, and $m_{4+}-(m_1+m_2+m_3)/3$. Under R's displayed scaling, the corresponding coefficients divide these differences by 2, 3, and 4. Thus we need both the coding weights and the coefficient to recover a named mean difference. We calculate the differences from the fitted MALD band means below.

```{r}
#| label: fit-mald-helmert-coding
library(ggplot2)

mald <- read.csv("data/mald/mald-items.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
mald$log_frequency_c <-
  mald$log_frequency_subtlex - mean(mald$log_frequency_subtlex)
mald$log_duration_c <- mald$log_duration - mean(mald$log_duration)
band_levels <- c(as.character(seq_len(3L)), "4+")
mald$syllable_band <- factor(
  ifelse(mald$n_syllables >= 4L, "4+", as.character(mald$n_syllables)),
  levels = band_levels
)
helmert_matrix <- contr.helmert(4)
rownames(helmert_matrix) <- levels(mald$syllable_band)
contrasts(mald$syllable_band) <- helmert_matrix

fit <- lm(
  mean_log_rt ~ syllable_band + log_frequency_c + log_duration_c,
  data = mald
)

helmert_matrix
coef(summary(fit))
```

The first Helmert coefficient is `r sprintf("%.4f", coef(fit)[["syllable_band1"]])`. Under the displayed scaling, twice this coefficient equals the fitted two-band minus one-band contrast at mean frequency and duration.

```{r}
#| label: plot-mald-helmert-coding
#| fig-cap: "Observed MALD item summaries and adjusted means for ordered syllable-count bands."
prediction_data <- data.frame(
  syllable_band = factor(
    levels(mald$syllable_band),
    levels = levels(mald$syllable_band)
  ),
  log_frequency_c = 0,
  log_duration_c = 0
)
interval <- predict(fit, newdata = prediction_data, interval = "confidence")
prediction_data$fit <- interval[, "fit"]
prediction_data$low <- interval[, "lwr"]
prediction_data$high <- interval[, "upr"]

helmert_comparisons <- data.frame(
  comparison = c(
    "two minus one",
    "three minus mean of one and two",
    "four-plus minus mean of earlier bands"
  ),
  fitted_mean_difference = c(
    prediction_data$fit[[2]] - prediction_data$fit[[1]],
    prediction_data$fit[[3]] - mean(prediction_data$fit[1:2]), # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
    prediction_data$fit[[4]] - mean(prediction_data$fit[1:3]) # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
  ),
  coefficient_times_scale = c(
    2 * coef(fit)[["syllable_band1"]],
    3 * coef(fit)[["syllable_band2"]],
    4 * coef(fit)[["syllable_band3"]]
  )
)
helmert_comparisons

point_opacity <- 0.06
ggplot(mald, aes(syllable_band, mean_log_rt)) +
  geom_jitter(color = "grey70", alpha = point_opacity, width = 0.16, height = 0, size = 0.55) +
  geom_pointrange(
    data = prediction_data,
    aes(y = fit, ymin = low, ymax = high),
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  labs(x = "Syllable-count band", y = "Mean log lexical-decision time") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

Each row in `helmert_comparisons` uses the adjusted means estimated from the observed MALD word items. The last two columns agree because the scaling factors recover exactly the comparisons named by the Helmert columns.

Two coding columns are **orthogonal** when their dot product, the sum of their rowwise products, equals zero. This algebraic property keeps the declared contrast directions perpendicular in the coded design. It gives us no guarantee that the observed item groups are balanced, statistically independent, or causally interpretable.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Which fitted means does the first Helmert column compare?
2. Why must coefficient magnitude be read from the displayed scaling?
3. Why is the four-or-more band not a one-unit step?
4. Does orthogonal coding make the linguistic predictors independent?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The first Helmert column compares the fitted two-syllable mean with the fitted one-syllable mean. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The coefficient multiplies the displayed contrast column; because the column has not been scaled to length one, the actual mean difference is twice the first coefficient. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The four-or-more-syllable band contains every item with at least four syllables, so its members differ internally and the boundary comparison is not a fixed one-syllable increment. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. No. Orthogonality is a property of the coding columns; it does not make observed item properties or groups statistically independent. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

We next use [reverse Helmert coding](inverse-helmert-coding.qmd) to reverse the direction of the successive grouping.
